item.title: Rescuers scramble for survivors with 180 dead in Colombia earthquake
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20dqd9qwq4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Rescuers scramble for survivors with 180 dead in Colombia earthquake - Published Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Monday's powerful earthquake. More than 180 people have been confirmed dead - most in the cities of Cali and Pereira. The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) on Monday and was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia - with fresh aftershocks still being felt on Tuesday. While the official death toll remains at 181, an aggregated figure gathered from local officials puts it higher - potentially at more than 240. A state of emergency has been declared by President Abelardo de la Espriella. Giving an update on Tuesday from Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, President Espriella said as well as those killed, almost 2,600 had been injured, and almost 200 people remain missing. He also reported that more than 1,100 homes had been destroyed, and more than 8,000 had been damaged. Overnight on Monday into Tuesday, several people spent the night outdoors in cities like Pereira and Cali - either due to their homes being destroyed, or fear of further collapses. Across the country, dozens of larger buildings have also collapsed. In Cali, a city of 2.2 million people where there have been 95 deaths, a unified command post has been set up to co-ordinate the rescue effort. On Tuesday, Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said that 239 people remained trapped, with 949 injured and 45 buildings which have either completely or partially collapsed. Several of the upper floors of one of the city's hospitals, some dedicated to paediatric care, collapsed, leaving some patients trapped. In Calima, a neighbourhood in the north of Cali, four children died after a section of the Gimnasio Calima school collapsed. The mayor of the municipality, Antonio Cadavid, stated that other children ended up with serious injuries, with a total of 30 children referred to care centres. To combat threats of looting, he has also ordered a curfew, coming into effect at 20:00 local time, and lasting until 06:00 on Wednesday morning. Further tremors were felt in Cali on Tuesday - part of a pattern of aftershocks across the country, with more than 70 having taken place since Monday's earthquake, according to Colombia's geological service. According to the agency, two earthquakes of magnitude 3.6 occurred early on Tuesday. The first was in San José del Palmar and the second in Santander. In Pereira, 79 people have died according to the city's fire department. The city has implemented a car-free day to allow the search to go ahead, with citizens urged to comply. Footage from the city has shown the massive scale of the rescue effort, with hundreds of volunteers working to remove rubble and free trapped survivors. Hours after the earthquake hit Pereira, a resident of the Parque Industrial neighborhood, near the city's airport, told BBC Mundo about the shock being experienced in the area. "It's impossible to get around the city center. In Bolívar Square (the city's main square), at least one building collapsed. Furthermore, there are structures where buses and trucks are trapped, and people are afraid those structures will collapse as well," he said. "We're all in shock. It was really awful." Jorge Eduardo Rojas, mayor of Manizales, said five people had been killed in the city. Sixty buildings in Manizales had partially or totally collapsed. Cautioning about further aftershocks, Rojas urged the public not to share chain messages or social media posts from unknown sources, as they "may contain false or unverified information... which could cause greater concern and alarm among the public". On Tuesday, help and support continued to be offered to Colombia from the international community. A statement from a spokesperson for UN Secretary-General, António Guterres, stated that he "expresses his solidarity with the people and government of Colombia" and that it working to support the government's response. Spain's Foreign Minister, José Manuel Albares, reported that 164 Spaniards were still missing. At the moment, he added, there are no reports of injuries or deaths of its citizens. The Trump administration, which backed President Abelardo de la Espriella in his successful election earlier this year, announced this afternoon a donation of $15.5m (£11.5m) to Colombia. Offers of help have also come from Ecuador, Brazil, El Salvador, and Venezuela. Related topics - Published1 day ago

item.title: Trump confirms he switched planes after Nato summit because of possible threat
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c980r4wpl9lo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump confirms he switched planes after Nato summit because of possible threat - Published President Donald Trump has confirmed that he secretly swapped planes as he left a Nato summit in Turkey last month due to a possible threat. "I go by Secret Service and the military. They wanted me to go in a different flight, different plane," Trump told reporters. "I just have to do what they say." The revelation comes after reports that Trump boarded Air Force One on 8 July in view of television cameras, before hiding in a catering truck to be transported to a military aircraft. The last-minute switch has raised questions about whether those left on the decoy plane were in danger, but Trump said on Tuesday the jet he boarded instead could have been at "greater risk... because that would be the plane, I think, that they would be more likely to go for." Officials told the BBC's US partner CBS News that the US had detected a credible Iranian threat to fire a missile at the plane. The New York Times reported that US intelligence had information of a person near the Nato summit who had been seen with a shoulder-fired missile. Journalists and some White House staff on board did not know the US president had been smuggled out as part of an elaborate ruse in response to a possible Iranian threat. Trump has previously said he was Iran's "number one target" during the summit in Ankara. "I guess there was a threat out there," the president said during a visit aboard Air Force One to an event in Ohio on Tuesday. "I didn't really ask too much about it. I get a lot of threats." He added: "I have a lot of threats that you don't know about." The clandestine manoeuvre last month came a day after the US renewed military strikes on Iran following a breakdown of negotiations between Washington and Tehran to end the war. Trump had arrived in Turkey aboard a newer Boeing 747-8 donated by Qatar, but announced that he would leave on the old Air Force One "for old time's sake". On 8 July, footage showed him boarding the presidential jet at Ankara airport. But according to the Washington Post, he slipped off Air Force One on to a catering truck that had been elevated to plane level on the opposite side to where he had boarded. He was then secretly taken to a smaller C-32A military aircraft - a modified Boeing 757 often used by the vice-president. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth boarded the C-32A separately using external stairs in an effort to make the flight appear normal, according to the newspaper. Journalists and some White House staff boarded Air Force One and were reportedly told to close their window shades. They were unaware the president was no longer on board. A media pool producer who was on the plane said they found it unusual when they were told to keep the window shades down. A photographer briefly opened a shade and reportedly was quickly told to close it. The producer's comments were detailed in a report from the White House Correspondents' Association on Tuesday. They also noted there appeared to have been two catering trucks at both the front and back of the plane when the press arrived, and that the media van had been too far back in the motorcade at the airport be able to take a photo of the president boarding. Technically "Air Force One" is the call sign for any aircraft carrying the US president. But on this occasion, the C-32A used the call sign "Reach 18", while the aircraft carrying the journalists continued to use "AF1" in order to keep up the ruse. Remaining on the original aircraft were members of Trump's cabinet, according to the New York Times. The outlet, citing two anonymous officials, reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were on board. Trump then flew to the UK en route to the US, where he reboarded the old Air Force One and was seen descending from the aircraft after it landed at RAF Mildenhall. It is unclear how he moved from the C-32A back to the legacy jet. - Trump's dramatic plane swap hints at personal stakes of Iran war - Published7 hours ago - Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight - Published10 hours ago The president then transferred to the new Qatari-donated Air Force One to travel back to Washington. During that flight, Trump spoke to reporters on board where he noted the threats posed by Iran but did not mention the earlier plane swap. Asked why reporters had been told to lower the window shades on the plane from Turkey, Trump said at the time: "Because you're probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleazebags we have to deal with." He said he had a "threat all the time" on his life, and that he is "number one" on Iran's "list". Jose Zamora, regional director for the Americas for the Committee to Protect Journalists, said in a statement that the Trump administration "has a responsibility to ensure that journalists covering the president are not unnecessarily exposed to danger". "Reporters should be informed of credible security threats so they can make informed decisions about their safety," he added. Additional reporting by Jessica Rawnsley

item.title: Trump's dramatic plane swap hints at personal stakes of Iran war
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly8jexn1z9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump's dramatic plane swap hints at personal stakes of Iran war - Published "I got him before he got me. They tried twice. Well, I got him first." That was President Donald Trump's observation, made to ABC correspondent Jonathan Karl, in a phone conversation the day after he launched the US military campaign against Iran in February. An Israeli airstrike, conducted with US approval and co-ordination, had just killed the Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other top Iranian leaders – and Trump drew a direct line from that attack to threats and alleged plots the Iranians had made against him in previous years. Trump has refrained from similar remarks in the ensuing six months of warfare, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has echoed the view. "Iran tried to kill President Trump, and President Trump got the last laugh," he said in March, noting that an unnamed Iranian who he said led an assassination unit had been killed in US strikes. These comments hint at the personal nature of this war – and the concerns by the president and his security team of the threat Iran still poses to his safety. Those concerns were dramatically illustrated by this week's revelation that Trump secretly switched to an alternate aircraft on his flight back from the Nato summit in Turkey last month. He left the media and most of the White House staff to depart on the presidential Air Force One 747 jet, which became, essentially, a decoy. It was an elaborate ruse, which included the president being transported to and from aircraft inside a catering truck, in response to what American officials reportedly believed to be credible intelligence of an Iranian missile threat to Air Force One. The White House has given little detail about this threat - but nonetheless it marks another striking episode in the turbulent history of Trump's relationship with Iran. Government security experts have said such measures are not unusual when a president travels in or near a warzone. Past presidents have travelled to places like Afghanistan, Iraq and Ukraine under cover of secrecy – but never without at least some prior knowledge by media outlets, under agreements that they would not disclose the movement until after the fact. The optics of Trump hiding in a catering truck from an apparent Iranian threat are less than ideal for a president who has repeatedly touted his strength - as well as the frailty of Iran's military after months of war. The secrecy in the days and weeks after the Secret Service operation in Ankara may have been, in part, to avoid undermining his public image of power. The operation, which took more than a month to come to light, also underscores the apparent threat Iran continues to present to US interests in a conflict that the president asserts is all but wrapped up against an adversary he has said has been thoroughly defeated on the battlefield. Iranian threats against Trump are not new, however. After Trump, in his first term, ordered the January 2020 missile strike that killed Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) leader Qasem Soleimani, Iran's leaders promised reprisals against the American president and senior administration leaders. In one instance, an Iranian mural depicted a drone targeting Trump while he played golf in Florida. It appears that there were more to these Iranian threats than just posturing. - Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight - Published10 hours ago - Trump hid in catering truck in secret plane swap over Iran threat, reports say - Published8 hours ago The Biden administration warned Iran in 2022 not to target any US citizens, after unearthing a plan to target former Trump National Security Adviser John Bolton. And in July 2024, US law enforcement arrested a Pakistani man, Asif Merchant, who allegedly had ties to the IRGC, for plotting to kill Trump. Four months later, an Afghani citizen, Farhad Shakeri, was charged with another assassination scheme against Trump. Merchant was convicted in March 2026, but Shakeri, who US prosecutors allege was directed by an IRGC official, is still at large. Although these attempts were foiled during the planning stages, the physical risks Trump faced as he sought a return to the White House were all too apparent. In July 2024 he was left bloodied after a gunman opened fire at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. Two months later, an armed man was arrested in Florida after US Secret Service agents spotted him hiding in the trees near where Trump was playing golf. "It was a galvanising moment for him," Maggie Haberman, a White House correspondent for the New York Times, said in a recent interview, external when discussing both the Iranian plots and assassination attempts of 2024. "All of that in his mind becomes one big blur." "For Trump himself, Iran and this feeling of being under threat is constant," she said. The president, according to the news website Semafor, external, often muses - and jokes - about becoming a target of assassination. "Nobody told me how dangerous it is to be president, and if they had told me, I probably wouldn't have run," one White House official recounted Trump as saying. "And he makes comments like that in jest, but there's a reality behind that." Trump's bombing of Iran's nuclear research facilities in 2025, and this year's expansive bombing campaign and naval blockade, prompted a new round of Iranian threats against Trump – and a direct warning by the US president in response. In July, Trump wrote on Truth Social that Iran had made threats "to assassinate, or attempt to assassinate" him and said 1,000 "missiles are Locked and Loaded and aimed at the Islamic Republic of Iran, with thousands more to immediately follow, should the Iranian Government act on its threat". The president's message to Iran was blunt. Many of the recent threats against him have been unequivocal, too. At the funeral service for Khamenei, held the day before Trump departed Turkey, participants carried a banner that read "#KillTrump". The following week, in a square in central Tehran, a building featured a large mural of the American president, lying in a black coffin, with the words "We will kill Trump" and "Blood for blood" written below it. Iran has denied involvement in any previous plots against Trump, but the message – delivered after Khamenei's death and reports of Iranian civilian casualties in US and Israeli strikes – has been clear. The war, Iranians are saying, is far from over. And Trump, himself, is a target for revenge. On the final leg of the journey back to the US from Turkey, as Trump and his travelling media pool were reunited on the same aircraft, the president came back to the press cabin to talk to reporters. They asked about the unusual journey, which included an order by the Secret Service that the window shades on the decoy plane be closed during takeoff from Ankara. "I have read all the time I'm number one on their list," he told them. "But if I go, you go, right?" Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here. Related topics - Published8 hours ago - Published9 November 2024

item.title: US says helicopter fired missiles to disable ship breaking Iran blockade
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvg8lyyyjedo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US says helicopter fired missiles to disable ship breaking Iran blockade - Published The US military says one of its helicopters has fired missiles to disable "the steering gear" of a cargo ship attempting to violate the US blockade of Iranian ports. In a statement, US Central Command (Centcom) says its MH-60 aircraft on Tuesday fired two hellfire missiles into the engine room of the Panama-flagged M/V Vela Nova vessel, as it attempted to transit the Gulf of Oman. Centcom said it acted after "the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings from American forces". The vessel "is no longer transiting to Iran", it added. Iran has not commented. The US has been enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports, following failed attempts to end the war it and Israel started on 28 February. Tehran retaliated by launching attacks on Israel and US-allied states across the Gulf. It has also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz - a key oil shipping waterway. A fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the strait before the war and prices have fluctuated wildly since then. Mediators have so far failed to bring the sides to an agreement on reopening the strait - and, since the latest ceasefire collapsed in June, both the US and Iran have exchanged fire intermittently. In its statement on X, Centcom said M/V Vela attempted to sail to an Iranian port without naming it. It also did not say whether there were any casualties or injuries. It says the US blockade "remains in full effect", adding that as of 11 August Centcom has "redirected 55 commercial vessels attempting to run the blockade, disabled 3 non-compliant vessels, and boarded 2". In a separate development on Tuesday, Yemen's internationally recognised government said six people were killed and 10 injured in strikes by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on a cargo ship in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they hit a vessel carrying Saudi military equipment. It appears to be the first deadly attack by the group on a ship since the war began. Related topics - Published8 hours ago

item.title: Cristiano Ronaldo marries long-time partner Georgina Rodríguez
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyj0325z3ko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Cristiano Ronaldo marries long-time partner Georgina Rodríguez - Published Football superstar Cristiano Ronaldo has married his longtime partner, model and influencer Georgina Rodríguez, in a civil ceremony in Portugal. The Portuguese striker posted an image on his Instagram account , externalshowing two hands, presumed to be his on top of his wife's, both wearing wedding rings. Calling it the wedding of the year, Portuguese media say the couple tied the knot on 11 August in the coastal town of Cascais near Lisbon - and that their five children attended. The Instagram entry had more than three million likes within 30 minutes of being posted. The couple have been together for 10 years, after they met at a Gucci shop in Madrid where Rodríguez was working. He was playing at the Spanish club Real Madrid at the time. They announced their engagement on 11 August last year. At the time, Rodríguez posted a picture of a large ring, writing "Yes I do. In this and in all my lives" in her native Spanish. Ronaldo has scored nearly 1,000 goals in a career in which he has played for Lisbon-based Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus, Al Nassr in Saudi Arabia and Portugal. He recently played in his sixth World Cup, a record for appearances in the men's finals which he shares with Lionel Messi of Argentina. - Published8 October 2025

item.title: At least 15 die as boat sinks in Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxe2vyxd7do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
At least 15 die as boat sinks in Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba - Published At least 15 people have died after a boat carrying dozens of people sank on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe, with rescue operations continuing., officials said Police said 90 passengers and five crew were onboard the vessel when it capsized on Tuesday, but it may have been overloaded, with other reports pointing to a higher number based on the registered ticket sales. The vessel was hit by a strong wave and overturned, police added. Footage shared online appears to show the hull floating in the water. Lake Kariba, which straddles the border with Zambia, is one of the world's largest man-made reservoirs, supporting transport and fishing and providing vital hydroelectric power to both countries. The Zimbabwe's Civil Protection Unit (CPU) said that registered ticket sales showed 114 adults were on board the vessel. There could also have been an unknown number of children below ticketing age, it added. "So far, 77 passengers have been rescued by Matusadonha rescue teams and others," the CPU said. It added that "15 bodies have also been retrieved", and two funeral parlours had been engaged to collect the bodies for processing. Mutsa Murombedzi, a local member of parliament, posted a video on X , externalof what she said was the boat at the start of the journey, adding that locals had been using it to travel across the lake to Kariba town, a journey that takes about five hours. "We have very hard questions that require honest answers. The officials must release the correct number of people who were onboard," she wrote. Police said more details would be released "in due course". item.title: Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8enj8p1xwgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Lebanon parliament votes to abolish death penalty - Published Lebanon's parliament has voted to abolish the death penalty, a move that would make it the first country in the Middle East to formally end capital punishment. A majority of MPs in the 128-seat parliament backed the measure on Tuesday, while Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc voted against it. The legislation will now go to the cabinet before being passed to President Joseph Aoun for signing. The government has already expressed its support for the measure. Lebanon has not carried out an execution since January 2004, although courts have continued to hand down death sentences. Rights groups estimate that more than 78 people remain on death row. Under the new legislation, capital punishment will be replaced with life imprisonment with hard labour. However, the legislation does not yet set out in detail how the new sentence would be enforced. Hard labour is already written into Lebanese law but has rarely been implemented in recent years. The country's financial crisis and overcrowded prisons have limited the authorities' resources and capacity. The latest legislation follows years of campaigning by civil society groups and lawyers for the removal of capital punishment from Lebanese law. "We cannot solve a crime with a crime or end violence with violence," Oragit Younan told the BBC. As co-founder of the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights, she led a nearly three-decade campaign to abolish the death penalty in Lebanon. "We are in a war, and people [have been] killed every day, so even in this situation, we can fight, we can struggle for human rights, and we can win. We can be a model for others," she said. Tuesday's vote in parliament follows more than two decades of a de facto moratorium on executions. An execution required a decree signed by the president, prime minister and justice minister - but no such decree has been signed since 2004. Under Lebanese law, the death penalty could previously be imposed for some of the country's most serious offences, including aggravated murder, certain terrorism-related crimes resulting in death, treason, espionage and offences against state security. Previous attempts to abolish the death penalty have failed, including legislation introduced in parliament in 2004 and a proposal from the justice ministry in 2008. Lebanon's move comes as the use of the death penalty remains contested elsewhere in the Middle East. Jordan resumed executions in June, carrying out its first since 2017. In Israel, its parliament has approved legislation that allows for the expansion of the circumstances in which capital punishment can be imposed. Israeli MPs passed a new law in May to impose the death penalty and conduct public trials for those involved in the Hamas-led attacks and mass hostage-taking in Israel in October 2023. Elsewhere, the UN human rights chief has said he is alarmed by the rise in executions in Iran, with capital punishment continuing to be used "to instil fear among the population and suppress dissent". In Iran, at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said earlier this month.

item.title: Bondi Beach shooting hero's assault charges dropped by police
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crk51ky7xzlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Bondi Beach shooting hero's assault charges dropped by police - Published A man who was hailed a hero for disarming one of the Bondi Beach shooters in December has had assault charges against him dropped by police. Ahmed al Ahmed was charged in June with domestic violence common assault, as well as stalking and intimidation, after an alleged incident with his father in March at a home in southwest Sydney. Ahmed denied both charges. On Wednesday, in a local Sydney court, prosecutors withdrew the charges after it was agreed that Ahmed would abide by an apprehended domestic violence order for 12 months, limiting his contact with his father. Outside the court, Ahmed, 44, welcomed the development, telling reporters that he was a "free man" and that he hoped for "peace". Defence lawyer Mohamed Sakr said in court that the order prohibiting Ahmed from assaulting, threatening, stalking or intimidating his father had been accepted without admissions, according to national broadcaster ABC. Ahmed made global headlines last year after footage emerged of him tackling one of two gunmen who had opened fire during a Jewish event at Sydney's Bondi Beach, killing 15 people. Ahmed wrestled a firearm from Sajid Akram and was later shot several times by a second alleged gunman, Naveed Akram. The attack marked Australia's deadliest mass shooting in decades, and police later declared it a terrorist incident targeting the Jewish community. A fundraiser in the days after the shooting raised more than AU$2.5m ($1.7m; £1.24m) for Ahmed, who also received a bedside visit from Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. In a separate court matter, two of Ahmed's brothers were recently charged over allegations they threatened him and tried to extort some of the donations he had received. Related topics - Published4 June

item.title: New Zealand PM survives second leadership challenge ahead of election
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2ve2jk5qeo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
New Zealand PM survives second leadership challenge ahead of election - Published New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has survived a vote of confidence before a general election due in November, saying he has the "full support" of his ruling National Party. Luxon had called for an "urgent" meeting with his National Party caucus on Wednesday to address "increased speculation about [his] leadership". "I have the full support of our caucus... Our caucus is united, and it is determined to win this election," he told reporters after the meeting which lasted more than three hours. This was the second challenge to his leadership in four months. Support for Luxon and his party remained weak amid sluggish economic growth and a series of missteps by the leader. Last week, Luxon drew backlash after suggesting a possible referendum on the country's electoral system on live radio, without prior consultation with his party colleagues. Earlier this month, the 56-year-old riled up New Zealand's business community after a speech calling on small business owners to "be adult". He said the country's businesses had a "parent-child mentality" with the central government and relied too often on handouts. He later apologised and acknowledged many were going through tough times. The former Air New Zealand boss led his centre-right party to victory in the 2023 elections vowing to bring down the cost of living and reduce taxes. "My pledge to you is that our government will deliver for every New Zealander," he said then. But his party has suffered in opinion polls in recent months as the economy continues to stall, with unemployment rising to an 11-year high of 5.6%. A 1News Verian poll published on Wednesday morning showed Luxon's preferred prime minister rating slide to 17% – a new low for his time in office – but he remains ahead of all other candidates included in the poll. New Zealand will hold its next general election on 7 November.

item.title: France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy5d11g72ppo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
France bans unsolicited telemarketing calls - Published France has banned unsolicited telemarketing phone calls, in what a consumer group is hailing as a "small revolution" for the sales industry. From Tuesday, unsolicited calls are prohibited for businesses in all sectors - but there are some exceptions. Calls will only be permitted if they relate to a contract a person has already entered into or the company has obtained prior consent to be contacted for marketing. "It cannot be stressed enough that peace and quiet is a right, and it is time to stop exposing consumers to unwanted solicitations," consumer advocacy group Que Choisir Ensemble, said in a statement. "This observation also holds true online and on the street, which are saturated with demands to consume," group president Marie-Amandine Stévenin added. She said the group had long been advocating "for an end to the automatic assumption that someone in their home or private life is a potential customer." "This is a victory for consumers, the vast majority of whom do not want to receive sales calls," she said. But the law change has riled some business groups, and officials in Morocco, where the call centre sector is heavily reliant on the French market. One government minister estimated the telemarketing restrictions could lead to the loss of up to 50,000 jobs, according to a report in Moroccan newspaper Le Matin. The head of France's direct-selling trade association, the Fédération de la Vente Directe (FVD), also criticised the reforms for adding what he said were administrative burdens for businesses. "You'll have to obtain written consent from your customer, and you'll also have to keep proof of that consent," Frédéric Billon said in comments reported by the New York Times. According to a 2025 parliamentary report, 97% of people are annoyed by telemarketing calls, with the authors wryly noting it is "one of those rare issues that unites people in France". The same report found 72% of French people reported being contacted on their mobile phones at least once a week, while 38% said they were called once a day. Germany, Austria and Italy are among the European countries that impose significant restrictions on telemarketing calls, often referred to as cold calls. In the UK, most telemarketing calls are legal provided the recipient has not objected to the call and their number is not on a statutory list of people or businesses who do not want to receive calls. item.title: Former judge removed by Orbán elected Hungarian president
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyed7rem5no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Former judge removed by Orbán elected Hungarian president - Published Hungary's parliament has elected András Baka, 73, a respected judge and former head of the Supreme Court, as head of state. The Hungarian president is a largely figurehead role, but Baka's rule promises to be tempestuous. His task will be to monitor Prime Minister Péter Magyar's efforts to dismantle the interlocking economic and political powerhouse established by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. He will also oversee the writing of a new constitution, to replace Orbán's constitution of 2011. "We cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," András Baka told Parliament, after he was elected by 140 votes to 6. "The majority of society now feels a sense of liberation and hope. Others feel disappointment and uncertainty," he said. "In a democratic society, this is not an anomaly, but a natural state of affairs." All 51 MPs belonging to Orbán's party Fidesz walked out of the chamber before the vote, in protest against the ousting of their favourite, Tamás Sulyok, from the post last month. In his speech, András Baka promised the broadest possible debate on the creation of a new constitution. Since taking office in early May, the new Magyar government has lost no time attacking Orbán's legacy. Twenty-seven laws have been passed, and two amendments to the constitution. The states of emergency - migrants, Covid, and war in Ukraine - which Orbán used to govern by decree, were all cancelled. The Sovereignty Protection Office, which the Fidesz government used to attack critical journalists and NGOs, was abolished, and an National Asset Recovery and Protection Office was established, with sweeping powers to investigate and prosecute individuals accused of stealing state funds under the former government. Fidesz accuses the Tisza government of establishing a "tyranny". Ironically, they removed Baka from his post as president of the Supreme Court in 2011, for attempting to stop them undermine the rule of law. Public service radio and TV have been off air since 9 July, as news programmes are revamped. The stated aim is to restore their independence, from their Fidesz-era role as government propaganda organs. Other key changes came under Amendments 16 and 17 of the constitution, limiting the prime minister to two terms in office, and MPs to three. The ability of the Constitutional Court to oversee acts of parliament, taken away by Fidesz, was also restored. If the Tisza majority expects Baka to be a tame president, they may get a rude awakening. In a BBC interview before he was asked to take the post, he made clear he opposes the limitation of MPs' terms as an intrusion on the right of voters to freely choose their representatives. Baka served for 17 years as the Hungarian judge at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. "I am not a political man," he told the BBC last month. "I got involved in politics through my professional, legal way of thinking." Baka was elected today as a transitional figure. Under the constitutional amendment which made his presidency possible, the new president will likely only be in place until the new constitution comes into force - or for maximum of five years. Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, Baka made it clear that he intended to push back against the Hungarian tendency to trust in powerful leaders. "The state is not there for itself," he said, at the end of his speech. "It is there for the people." Related topics - Published14 April - Published13 April

item.title: These seaside apartments were a ghost city - then police say scammers moved in
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2kvlye1k5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
These seaside apartments were a ghost city - then police say scammers moved in - Published From a distance, Malaysia's Forest City looks 3D-printed: a bristle of identical white blocks clustered on an otherwise unremarkable coastline. When it was unveiled by Chinese developers in 2016, the $100bn mega-project was pitched as "a dream paradise for all mankind": a special financial zone that could house some 700,000 residents. But a decade later, this 14-sq-km (3,400-acre) artificial island on Singapore's doorstep is thought to be inhabited by less than 1% of that. Rows of eerily vacant skyscrapers loom over quiet streets. Inside empty apartments, benchtops and windows are filmed with dust. "In 2016 they described it here like the golden city; very, very beautiful," says Jason Deng, a 56-year-old investor who was among the first to buy in Forest City, paying "a lot of money" for five properties. "If I had known it was not so good I would not have bought so many apartments," he says now. "I thought it would be much, much better." As it turns out, this is only a golden city for some people – and they're not the ones developers had hoped to attract. In mid-July, Malaysian police raided two alleged scam operations spread across 32 premises in Forest City, arresting 335 people and seizing assets worth about one million ringgit (£181,810; $245,000), including 313 computers, 1,557 mobile phones, 17 laptops and 10 modems. From these two call centre hubs – one occupying 27 apartments across five storeys of a residential tower, the other spread between five bungalows – cryptocurrency syndicates ran investment and love scams targeting victims abroad, according to police. Those arrested include 309 Chinese nationals, 19 Indonesians, three Malaysians and four Myanmar nationals. Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said authorities were working with Interpol to track down the mastermind behind the operations. The BBC reached out to Forest City and Johor police for comment, but did not receive a response. Experts and locals tell the BBC this is likely to be the tip of the iceberg – and a symptom of a global scam industry that is spreading, evolving, and professionalising. "The reality is that many of these organisations now resemble multinational corporations more than a traditional organised crime network or gang," says John Wojcik, an analyst at TRM Labs, which investigates crypto-facilitated crime. "They have dedicated recruitment teams, IT departments, money-laundering specialists and infrastructure." Authorities and experts agree that the Forest City operations were probably staffed by criminals who had been driven out of Cambodia, a global nerve centre for transnational scams. Over the past five years, this criminal sector has ballooned into a multi-billion-dollar industry, built on the forced labour of brutalised trafficking victims who work under threat of torture and abuse. Since late last year, the Cambodian government has stepped up efforts to stamp out these operations. Authorities recently estimated that 300,000 people had left the country within a few months as raids on industrial-scale compounds intensified. But these Malaysian offshoots do not appear to have been scam "compounds" in the traditional sense. Compared to more infamous walled complexes in places like Sihanoukville or the Myanmar borderlands, the alleged scam hubs in Forest City appear almost white collar, reportedly staffed by local residents and sitting wall-to-wall with the homes of unsuspecting neighbours. Kevin, a tenant who also works in property sales for Forest City, believes scammers are still operating in "condominiums or serviced apartments" in the complex. He asked for his name to be changed for fear of repercussions. "We know what they're doing," he says. "This is actually a very common issue in Johor city and Kuala Lumpur, but especially in Forest City. Forest City is very special." Part of what makes Forest City "special", according to Kevin, Wojcik and others, is the very thing that has gained it so much notoriety: its reputation as a semi-abandoned "ghost city". "When we speak to clients or customers, the company teaches us to say 'we already have 23,000 residents living in this area'," says Kevin – but the reality, he quietly adds, is there are "less than 5,000". "That's the reason" scammers have chosen Forest City to set up shop, he suggests. "They have their own privacy... Nobody comes here." There are several factors which precipitated what many see as the downfall of Forest City. Spearheaded by Country Garden, one of China's largest property developers, and Danga 88, a private company controlled by Malaysian Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, the project was initially dreamed up as an eco-friendly metropolis for well-heeled Chinese clients. Featuring a high-end hotel, golf course and water park, the resort-style city's seafront offices and apartments were expected to be in high demand. But the combined weight of the Covid pandemic, China's spiralling property slump and constricted borrowing limits for its citizens have sunk those sky-high ambitions, and all but ground the project to a standstill. The lights are still on, but almost no-one is home. And that appears to have made the complex a honeypot for scammers. "Forest City reflects the conditions organised crime have been targeting for years - a flagship location marketed as a prestigious, luxury, master-planned smart city that never came close to fulfilling that vision," Wojcik says. "Developments like this offer precisely what these syndicates look for: modern infrastructure, large numbers of vacant properties, and international connectivity all wrapped around the veneer of legitimate economic activity to ensure that the criminal nature of what goes on inside remains unnoticed." With this in mind, the glittering facade of Forest City echoes a more infamous metropolis 1,800 kilometres (1,120 miles) to the north: Shwe Kokko, the so-called resort city on Myanmar's Thai border, which is one of the world's most notorious scam hubs. Built by the private Chinese conglomerate Yatai, Shwe Kokko markets itself as a safe holiday destination for Chinese tourists and a haven for the super-rich. But behind its tree-lined streets and luxury villas is a nexus of fraud, money-laundering and human trafficking. For all its headwinds, and despite the fact that only 15 to 20% of the originally proposed project has been completed, Forest City similarly still markets itself as an up-and-coming hotbed for property investment, tech innovation and tax-free business ventures. Such entrepreneurial packaging serves as a Trojan horse for scammers wanting to set up shop without drawing unwanted attention – and allows them to perpetrate their fraud more effectively. Wojcik explains that "when scam syndicates can embed themselves behind seemingly legitimate businesses in ordinary commercial developments, they not only become more difficult to detect and disrupt, they become capable of exerting serious amounts of power and influence through the massive profits they generate". This power and influence in turn allows scammers to professionalise in other ways. Though human trafficking still largely fuels much of the scam industry's labour force, there is now a noticeable trend of syndicate operators recruiting and retaining experienced scammers with higher pay and better working conditions. Meanwhile, in the same Telegram groups where scam jobs are being advertised, career scammers are also now posting detailed resumes, outlining their experience in fraudulent activities and emphasising their eagerness to work. "It's a sign the industry is maturing into a more professionalised criminal enterprise," Wojcik explains, "while coercion and exploitation still remain widespread". The Forest City raids highlight a transnational scam industry that is shifting in size and shape. But this is far from the first time such operations have been detected in Malaysia. Throughout 2022, before the industry gained widespread global attention, Malaysian authorities raided several scam centres operating out of bungalows and condominiums in the southern state of Johor, the northern state of Penang and the capital city of Kuala Lumpur. Yet while these and other major crackdowns sent a message of zero tolerance to fraud syndicates, Wojcik notes that Malaysia has remained home to influential criminal networks - and that "any signs of large-scale re-emergence deserve close attention". In Forest City, such signs may already be emerging. Kevin says it's long been an "open secret" that scams are happening here, and that "the only shocking thing is that the police were effective". He's certain there are more, too – but is unperturbed at the idea that his neighbours might be defrauding people out of hundreds of thousands of dollars. "For me, I don't care," he says. "It's not my business... I work here just for the salary." Other residents feel the same way. Phillip, whose name we have also changed, moved to Forest City from Singapore last year, attracted by the relatively cheap property market and the idea that he could get more value for his money. He works in tech, and says he is "very focused" on the topic of cyber protection. "Yes they [the scammers] might be on my doorstep, they might be my neighbours... [they] could be one of the ones that's running one of these syndicates. At the end of the day, it doesn't matter where you go – this is going to happen." He says he was "not surprised" to hear about the reports of scam centres in his complex. What has surprised him is the fact that "more and more people are moving" to Forest City. One of the reasons he chose the development where he lives is because of the peace and quiet, he says – but he's pleased to see that it is evolving from a "ghost town" into a place where people seem to want to be. "So many people have lost money on these developments," he points out. "But the last three months, you see the lights on in the condos. You've gone from one in 20 to maybe one in five." - Published5 December 2023 - Published23 November 2023 - Published6 February 2025

item.title: Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9d84874dzjo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight - Published On 8 July, US President Donald Trump boarded Air Force One in plain sight of television cameras as he departed the Nato summit in Turkey. But when the mighty Boeing aircraft left Ankara, the president had reportedly already been secretly spirited away via a catering truck to a C-32A, a military version of the Boeing 757, which flew the president to RAF Mildenhall in the UK. Those left on board were unwitting decoys and had no indication that Trump was no longer travelling with them. But deception of this kind is not unusual. "That's very common," said Ronald Kessler, an author who has written extensively on the agency. "There's a long history of strategies to mislead anybody who might be trying to harm the president." Robert McDonald, a former high-ranking Secret Service agent with experience working on presidential security details, told the BBC that smaller-scale deceptions are used frequently during motorcade operations. These motorcades - which often include dozens of security and support vehicles, as well as ambulances and vans carrying White House reporters - typically include two "Beasts", as the enhanced limousine carrying the president is known. While one vehicle carries the president, the other travels nearby as a decoy, switching locations while en route to the destination. "It's what we call a shell game," said McDonald, who drove one of the vehicles during President George W Bush's administration. "Even in DC if we headed to Andrews [Joint Base Andrews - where Air Force One flies from], those two limousines would change position, like under a highway overpass." "But that would happen out of sight of anybody other than those in the motorcade or in that tunnel," he added. "Different things are used to mix up the bad guy." Similarly, Marine One - the president's helicopter - routinely flies in groups of three, changing positions so that potential threats are not sure which is carrying the US leader. Even more elaborate deceptions are carried out for complex, high-risk trips abroad. "I would say it does not happen often," former Secret Service agent Paul Eckloff told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme of the aircraft switch. "But it is an option that the Secret Service and others in executive protection always have." "When the president travels to war zones, there are frequently tactics and techniques used to create doubt in an adversary of which aircraft or which movement that he's going to make," he added. In March 2000, for example, then-President Bill Clinton flew from India to the Pakistani capital of Islamabad on an unmarked executive jet that landed after a decoy jet with all the livery of Air Force One. Three years later, the White House claimed that George W Bush would spend Thanksgiving in Texas, only to arrive in Baghdad in a blacked-out Air Force One. In 2023, Joe Biden also was secretly taken to Ukraine with a slimmed down press pool of one reporter and one photographer. In all three of those cases, the media on board was aware of the deception but had been asked to not report it in real time. The exact nature of the perceived threat to the aircraft in this latest case remains unclear. The Secret Service has so far not commented on the incident, while the White House has neither confirmed nor denied it, saying only that it uses every tool available to protect the president. While contingency plans for a variety of scenarios are developed ahead of time, experts say that the Secret Service needs to maintain flexibility and remain poised to improvise in the face of new threats as they emerge, particularly overseas. But according to McDonald, the extraordinary measure of secretly moving President Trump from the aircraft suggests that the potential danger was deemed, likely by multiple agencies, to be serious. "That tells me that the threat level in Turkey was relatively substantial and quite high," he said, adding that the president's staff, the Secret Service and the White House Military Office were almost certainly immediately alerted. "Those people likely got together in a room and were presented with this intelligence," McDonald explained. "And a plan was put together to negate the threat from whatever intelligence was received." McDonald's assessment was echoed by Marc Polymeropoulos, a 26-year veteran of the CIA who served in both Iraq and Afghanistan and oversaw clandestine missions around the world. "The key part of this is the nature of the threat, and what was so severe that the Secret Service would put forth such a deception operation," he said. A key question going forward, according to Polymeropoulos, is whether the government and intelligence community then had a duty to warn those on the aircraft. "Let's say the plane was blown out of the sky, and we knew about it," he said. "We don't do that…we can't. If we know ISIS is going to attack a target in Moscow, we warn the Russians. Why do we warn the Russians? Because if there's an American citizen killed in that, we can't let that happen." How much danger those who remained on the aircraft were in - or whether they were in danger at all - remains unclear. Journalists on board reported that they were repeatedly instructed to keep their window blinds down, a "not uncommon" practice McDonald said shows that steps were still being taken to protect the passengers. "A large plane flying overhead where somebody could see it, with the shades up and windows illuminated, could tell somebody that it's a particular type of aircraft," he said. "I appreciate the need for transparency, but [the passengers] are also part of the roadshow. We've got to make sure that you and everybody gets home safe." The Secret Service, he added, is under no legal obligation to inform of potential threats or detail operations being carried out to protect the president and his entourage. That decision would need to be made by the White House or other agencies. "The Secret Service is not in the business of public relations," he said. "We're very good at keeping secrets, as our name says. Everybody doesn't need to know everything." Related topics - Published8 hours ago

item.title: Anguish of Colombian brother at rubble of building being searched for earthquake survivors
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxerlglgw5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Anguish of Colombian brother at rubble of building being searched for earthquake survivors - Published Efraín Gallego does not lose faith that his brother will be found alive, although when he speaks about him, trapped beneath the rubble of a building, his voice breaks and he swallows hard until he regains his composure. "You feel anguish. Every time there is an alert about someone being alive, hope is reborn that we will find him," Gallego tells me emotionally. His 80-year-old brother was buried along with his wife when the Torres del Limonar building collapsed in Cali. This city in south-western Colombia is one of the hardest hit by the earthquake. The building has become a symbol of the tragedy in the country's third most populous city. Cali has more than two million inhabitants. According to Mayor Alejandro Éder, there are at least 95 dead. Under the scorching heat on Tuesday morning, Torres del Limonar is a shattered mountain of rubble, with mattresses, furniture, and belongings peeking out from the concrete. On top of the remains are rescuers and volunteers: "Silence! We are firefighters. If you can hear us, shout or make any noise." The phrase is repeated every time the teams dig deep enough to believe they may be close to a survivor. These are the moments when Gallego regains hope, but the seconds pass and no answers come from below. Torres del Limonar is one of more than 50 collapsed buildings in Cali. It is located in its south, in the Capri neighbourhood. The four-storey building held dozens of apartments. The exact number of tenants who were inside when it collapsed is unknown. Around it, apart from some cracks, the rest of the buildings seem to have escaped the fate of the Torres. Rescuers, military personnel, volunteers, paramedics, firefighters, humanitarian workers, and journalists have come here. There are more than 100 people waiting for news. According to Mayor Éder, as of Monday night, it was estimated that 25 people were trapped under the rubble. Éder declared a nighttime curfew to speed up rescue operations. The night passed. Excavations continue. A rescuer at the site said about 10 people had been saved since the collapse. Reports in local media, such as one from Blu Pacífico radio, spoke of six survivors up until a few minutes before my arrival, including an infant only a few months old. In the midst of tragedy, figures are often closer to estimates than definitive data. "What I can tell you is that right now there are at least two people detected alive. Tunnels are being made to get them out. One of them has to have his leg freed," rescuer James Velasco tells me. The magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck Colombia on Monday, 10 August, is the worst in this century, according to the National Geological Service. In addition to Cali, it left destruction and death in other regions such as Chocó, in the north-west. Around the remains of Torres del Limonar, unlike Gallego, many residents choose not to speak. They are visibly affected. Some sleep exhausted on the ground or on a sofa placed in the street. Others gather together under the shade for support. The hours are long, increasingly so, and the anguish grows. Velasco offers hope. "In the past I have participated in operations where we have pulled out survivors after seven days trapped." "Those who are meant to survive, survive. Nothing is written," he adds. "I wanted to help from the very beginning." Amid his anguish, Gallego wants to acknowledge the work of ordinary citizens. "We must mention all the people who have come to help with water, supplies, tools, equipment; there is a lot of collaboration. Volunteers are plentiful," he says. Alejandro Mahecha, 19, is one of those volunteers. He decided to come after spending the night safely with his family and overcoming the initial shock. "I wanted to help from the very beginning. The earthquake affected my city and the homes of people I know. I came to this site because there has been a lot of talk about this building and the need for help here," the young man explains. Together with several friends, Mahecha helps remove rubble, bring water to rescuers, and clear the street to facilitate evacuation efforts. In the background, hammers and saws can be heard creating escape routes through the destruction. They stop only when those present raise their arms. That means everyone must remain silent. Gallego waits. This time, too, there was no news of his brother. Related topics - Published12 hours ago

item.title: How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana log raft
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye8332d63o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana log raft - Published Well past midnight on 19 July, as floodwaters surged through a village in India's northeastern state of Assam, Bornali Baruah and her husband were trying to save his 97-year-old mother. Almost bedridden, Lokada Duarah could not walk. There was no boat, no rescue team and no neighbour available to help. So they lifted her onto a makeshift raft made of banana trunks, and carried her through the rushing water towards safety. "Everyone was trying to save themselves," Baruah says. An hour later, she says, the three of them reached a shelter camp on a national highway some distance away from their house in Charing village in Sivasagar district, one of the worst flood-affected districts. The water was three to four feet deep and the current so strong that they had to move slowly, holding each other's hands and using sticks to steady themselves. By then, Baruah's home was disappearing beneath the flood. The water would eventually rise to about five feet inside it. The scene in Charing was part of a much wider disaster unfolding across Assam. The latest figures put the death toll from floods at 100, with 10 districts and 456 villages affected and about 140,000 people impacted. Fifty-two relief camps have been set up. Overall, the floods have affected nearly 1.2 million people across 25 districts, damaged more than 19,000 houses and left more than 75,000 people in 252 relief camps. The floods have been particularly severe in parts of Upper Assam, where villages like Charing that do not usually flood have been inundated. For Baruah, 40, the shock is especially profound. "This is the first flood we have experienced in this area in our lifetime," she says. Baruah has lived in Charing since birth, and her ancestors lived here before her. She recalls hearing about a major flood in 1950, long before she was born, but nothing like this had happened during her lifetime. Her home sits in a landscape criss-crossed by rivers, though none runs immediately beside it. The single-storey, eight-room house is about 25km (15 miles) from Sivasagar town; the Brahmaputra is roughly 20km away, the Dikhow 12km, the Jhanji 10km and the Mitong just 5km. She had never imagined the water would reach her doorstep. But when it did, the flood threatened not only her home, but the livelihood she had spent years building. Baruah was once a full-time journalist. In 2016, she left the profession to take up animal husbandry, and three years later was named Assam's 'Best Livestock Farmer'. Her farm grew to around 300 goats, 500 ducks and 1,000 chickens, along with fish. The flood destroyed much of it. She says she lost most of her goats, 300 ducks, 300 chickens and a sizeable amount of fish, as well as the machine she used to make animal feed. Furniture, laptops, vehicles and the family's collection of books were also destroyed. None of her livestock was insured. "There is no insurance system here for livestock, especially goats," she says. The first warning came on 17 July, when the Jhanji river began to rise. Two days later, the Dikhow and Mitong spilled into surrounding areas as the Brahmaputra and its tributaries swelled rapidly. Several rivers breached their embankments, Baruah says, sending powerful currents through towns and villages. About a day after the water began rising, she and her family abandoned their home. By then, the water inside the house was four feet deep. They spent the next 10 days in a relief camp. For five days in the camp there was no electricity or mobile connectivity and Baruah could not even charge her phone. The government provided the family with a relief kit containing rice, lentils and cooking oil. Help also came from strangers at the camp. A young woman whom Bornali had never met, helped with food, cleaning and looking after her 60 surviving goats. Another took responsibility for treating and feeding animals that had fallen ill. But why did the water reach a place that Baruah says had never flooded before? Dhrubajyoti Sahariah, a professor of geography and director of the Centre for Brahmaputra Studies at Gauhati University, says flooding itself is natural in the Brahmaputra Valley, a lowland region in Assam. What has changed is the "frequency, intensity and severity of floods well beyond historical norms". The Brahmaputra, one of the world's largest multi-channel rivers, ranks among the top five globally for both water discharge and sediment load. Much of that sediment comes from Tibet, where the river originates. As it enters Assam's vast floodplains, home to some 28 million people and hemmed in by hills, it slows and deposits sediment, fuelling erosion and floods. Flooding is an annual feature of life in Assam, but some years are far worse: the 2004 floods alone affected 12 million people and killed 251. In the recent floods, Sahariah says, continuous heavy rainfall in Upper Assam and neighbouring Nagaland's Mon district triggered severe flooding and large-scale silt deposition in Sivasagar, Charaideo and Jorhat. Sahariah says floods are reaching areas once spared because more people have settled on active floodplains, forests have been cleared, mining and hill-cutting have increased sediment in rivers, and roads, bridges and other infrastructure have been built without adequately accounting for the region's hydrology. Yet Assam cannot manage the Brahmaputra on its own. Many of its tributaries originate in the surrounding hill states, while flood-control measures are largely planned within Assam. "What is needed is basin-scale planning," Sahariah says, along with greater coordination between states and better understanding of the rivers' changing geography. For Baruah, however, the science has become painfully personal. She has returned to the area around her flood-damaged home. For now, she and her family are staying at a neighbour's house nearby, hoping to move back into their own home within a week. Baruah says she does not intend to leave Charing. Moving away, she says, requires economic and social circumstances that her family simply does not have. So she is beginning to think about how to live with a threat that was, until now, largely absent from her life. She says that if heavy rain comes again, she would need to raise the house higher, perhaps by building up its foundation. She is not yet sure how she would manage it or pay for it. The family would also need a raised platform where they could retreat to safety, and they would stock food and drinking water in advance. Baruah is learning to live with the possibility of more floods – and to prepare for them. Did she feel like a climate refugee? "No. If we regain our economic and mental strength, life will return to the way it was before." "We will have to learn to coexist with the floods."

item.title: Watch: What is it like to travel on Air Force One with Trump?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cy4k1jldxnwo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Watch: What is it like to travel on Air Force One with Trump? President Donald Trump secretly swapped planes as he left a Nato summit in Turkey last month, according to US media. Footage from 8 July shows him boarding Air Force One, the presidential jet, at Ankara airport. But according to the Washington Post, he was then secretly taken to a smaller C-32A military aircraft - a modified Boeing 757 often used by the vice-president - via a catering truck, which had been elevated to plane level on the opposite side to where he had boarded. Journalists and some White House staff boarded Air Force One and were reportedly told to close their window shades. They were unaware the president was no longer on board. The BBC's State Department correspondent Tom Bateman shares what it's like to be onboard Air Force One with the president as part of the press pool. Read more about the story here. Watch: Why was Trump smuggled out of Air Force One in a catering truck? Donald Trump secretly switched planes when he was returning from a Nato meeting last month in order to avoid a threat to his life from Iran, US media has reported. The president boarded Air Force One in Ankara, Turkey, on 8 July before being transported to another aircraft with the help of a catering truck, the Washington Post said. He was then seen disembarking Air Force One in the UK, before boarding his newer, Qatari-gifted jet and returning to the US. Trump spoke to journalists during his flight to the US but did not say whether he had been moved to a different plane. Watch: Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river Workers waded through a rubbish-filled river in Manila, collecting waste that washed in during days of heavy rain. The nine-day downpour, exacerbated by tropical storms, was equivalent to more than a month's worth of rain in some areas. It resulted in school and government office closures across the main island of Luzon and flooding in the capital.
